text: Filler words such as 'um', 'uh', and 'like' are speech disfluencies. Frequent use tends to lower listeners' perception of a speaker's confidence and competence, even when the content is strong.
source: Communication research — speech disfluency perception (placeholder paraphrase)

text: A practical technique for reducing fillers is to replace them with a brief silent pause. Pausing gives the speaker time to think and the audience time to absorb, without signalling hesitation the way a filler does.
source: Toastmasters International — reducing filler words (placeholder paraphrase)

text: Filler frequency rises under cognitive load and nervousness. Rehearsing transitions between points — the moments where fillers cluster — measurably reduces their rate.
source: Communication research — disfluency and cognitive load (placeholder paraphrase)

text: A conversational speaking rate of roughly 120 to 150 words per minute is generally comfortable for listeners to follow. Sustained rates well above this can outpace comprehension.
source: Toastmasters International — vocal delivery and pace (placeholder paraphrase)

text: Speaking too slowly can reduce perceived energy and let attention drift, while speaking too quickly can bury key points. Varying pace intentionally — slowing for emphasis — is more effective than a single constant speed.
source: Communication research — speech rate and comprehension (placeholder paraphrase)

text: Strategic pauses are part of good pacing. A short pause before or after an important point increases its impact and gives listeners a moment to process, whereas many long unplanned pauses can signal loss of structure.
source: Toastmasters International — pauses and pacing (placeholder paraphrase)
